A.explanation: V does not increase. Closing S causes current and lost volts in $r$, so terminal p.d. $V$ falls below $E$.

B.explanation: Closing S allows current $I$, so a p.d. $Ir$ is lost across $r$ and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ decreases.

C.explanation: V is only across the cell between P and Q, not across $r$ plus $R$, so there is no such balancing to keep V constant.

D.explanation: Although $E$ equals the sum of p.d.s around the loop when closed, $V$ is the terminal p.d. across the cell only and it falls.

hints: Notice that P and Q are the terminals of the cell containing $E$ and $r$, so $V$ is the terminal p.d. of the cell.
Compare the current when S is open with the current when S is closed through $R$ and $r$.
Recall $V = E - Ir$ for a cell supplying current $I$, where $Ir$ is the p.d. lost across internal resistance $r$.
walkthrough: Identify $V$: from the diagram $V$ is measured between P and Q, which are the two terminals of the real cell modelled by $E$ in series with $r$.
When S is open there is no complete circuit, so current $I = 0$ and no p.d. is lost across $r$. Hence $V = E$.
When S is closed a series circuit of $r$ and $R$ is formed, so a current $I = E/(R+r)$ flows through both $r$ and $R$.
Apply the terminal p.d. rule $V = E - Ir$. The term $Ir$ is the lost volts across internal resistance $r$ when current flows.
Since $Ir > 0$ when closed, $V$ changes from $E$ to $E - Ir$ and therefore decreases. This is option B.
